maths.problem: In the Juice Test, 8 of the 10 washed seeds in Box W sprouted. Only 1 of the 10 seeds in Box J sprouted. How many times as many seeds sprouted in Box W?
maths.explain: Box W had 8 sprouted seeds and Box J had 1. 8 divided by 1 is 8. So 8 times as many seeds sprouted in water as in juice.
maths.context: This is about the Juice Test, where you put washed tomato seeds on water in Box W and seeds on tomato juice in Box J.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'more sprouted in water' is true, but 'eight times as many' shows how big the difference really is.

maths.problem: Farhan counted the sprouted seeds in Box W each day. Day 3: 2. Day 4: 5. Day 5: 7. Day 6: 7. Day 7: 7. He had 10 seeds. Why did the count stop at 7? Give two possible reasons.
maths.answer: Three seeds never sprouted. They may have been damaged or dead, or not yet ripe enough when the tomato was picked.
maths.explain: The count went up by 3, then 2, then stopped. All the seeds had the same water and warmth, so the 3 seeds that never sprouted were probably different themselves. Some seeds in any fruit are damaged, empty or not fully grown. This is why we use 10 seeds, not 1.
maths.context: This is about the Juice Test. You count the washed tomato seeds with roots every day for a week.
maths.why_maths: Spotting where a pattern stops tells you something: here, that some seeds were different from the rest.

maths.problem: Charles Darwin predicted the long-tongued moth of Madagascar in 1862. Scientists described the moth in 1903. How many years did people wait? Darwin died in 1882. How many years after his death was the moth described?
maths.explain: 1903 take away 1862. 1862 plus 40 is 1902, plus 1 more is 1903. So 41 years. Then 1903 take away 1882. 1882 plus 20 is 1902, plus 1 is 1903. So 21 years.
maths.context: This is about Darwin's orchid, a flower in Madagascar whose nectar lies at the bottom of a very long tube.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting dates shows how long a prediction can wait before anyone can check it.

maths.problem: In the Juice Test, 8 of 10 washed seeds sprouted. In Waiting or Dead, 6 of the 9 washed juice seeds sprouted. Did more than half sprout each time?
maths.explain: Half of 10 is 5, and 8 is more than 5. Half of 9 is four and a half, and 6 is more than four and a half. So more than half sprouted both times. That means the juice seeds were mostly alive, just waiting.
maths.context: This is about the Juice Test and the Waiting or Dead test, where you washed the seeds that had sat in tomato juice and put them on water.
maths.why_maths: The two tests had different numbers of seeds, so comparing with half is fairer than comparing the counts.

warmup.q: Name one thing plants give animals.
What does a bee carry from flower to flower?
What is the sweet juice in flowers called?
Why don't tomato seeds sprout inside the tomato?
Which tiny animal pollinates a fig?
Who planted the peepal on the wall?
warmup.a: A bird, by dropping a seed.

roots.context: We have learned how plants and animals feed, shelter and carry each other, and why seeds wait inside a fruit. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Tomato seeds lying in their own juice did not sprout, but washed seeds sprouted within a week. So inside a fruit, the juice holds the seeds back. They start growing once the fruit is eaten by an animal or rots away. Plants cannot carry their seeds far away, so they feed animals who will.
deep_truth.habit: We think of each plant and each animal as living a separate life, inside their own body. But a tomato plant's young begin their lives only after an animal, or rot, takes the fruit away. Part of a plant's life is lived through the animals who eat her fruit.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Juice Test, seeds in tomato juice did not sprout, while washed seeds from the same tomato did. In Waiting or Dead, the juice seeds sprouted once they were washed. So the seeds were alive, waiting for the flesh to go.

three.who_am_i: Every meal you eat began with a plant. Each time you eat a guava or a tomato, you are the animal her seeds were waiting for.
three.what_is_life: No life is lived alone. A peepal seedling on a wall needed a wasp, a bird and the rain before she could grow.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of partners, near and far. An orchid in Madagascar and her moth fit each other, just as the peepal fits her tiny wasp.

roots.thread: A tomato plant, a bird and a fig wasp each live in their own body. Yet the tomato's fruit is shaped for an eater's mouth, and the fig's tiny hole is shaped for one kind of wasp. Each body carries a part of another's life. These partners grew to fit each other over millions of years, and all of them came from the same first living cells. So many different lives turn out to be parts of one long, shared story of life.

teachings.link: In this unit, the fig feeds the wasp's young and the wasp makes the fig's seeds. The tomato feeds an animal, and the animal carries her seeds to a new place.

teachings.source: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1859), the last paragraph
teachings.teaching: Darwin asks us to look at a tangled bank of plants, with birds singing, insects flying and worms crawling, and to see how different they are, and how closely they depend on each other.
teachings.link: Three years later, the same Darwin looked at one orchid's long tube and knew, from that dependence alone, that a long-tongued moth must exist.

science.text: Animals carry the pollen of about 87 in every 100 kinds of flowering plants.
Fig trees and fig wasps have depended on each other for at least 34 million years, as fossil wasps show.
Plants sense their animal visitors and respond, for example by making sweeter nectar when they hear a bee. How widely this happens is still being tested.

other_view.view: Plants and animals do not help each other out of kindness. Each one does what keeps herself and her young alive, and the help is a side effect. A bee takes nectar for her colony, and the pollen she carries is an accident. On this view, partnerships are explained fully by natural selection, with no need for any shared story of oneness.

practice.title: Thank the helpers in a fruit
practice.say: Let's each hold a piece of fruit, like a banana or a guava. Close your eyes and take three slow breaths. Now, with your eyes still closed, name one living thing that helped make this fruit. Then name another. The plant who grew her. The bee or the fly who carried pollen. The worms in the soil. The farmer. Take one more slow breath. Now eat the fruit slowly.
practice.kid: Hold a piece of fruit. Close your eyes. Breathe slowly three times. Name a helper who made this fruit. Name another. Now eat it slowly.

ask: A bee takes nectar to feed her own family. If she doesn't mean to help the flower, is she still helping?
A plant offers a fruit, and an animal carries her seeds. Is that a gift, a trade, or something else?
The tomato seeds were waiting for an eater. Is a seed's life her own, or partly the eater's?

how_we_found_out.story: In 1977, an American scientist named Stanley Temple made a famous claim. On the island of Mauritius grows a tree called the tambalacoque. Temple said only 13 old trees were left, and no young ones. The dodo, a big bird that could not fly, lived only on Mauritius, and had died out about 300 years before. Temple said the tree's seeds could sprout only after passing through a dodo's gut. To test it, he fed 17 tambalacoque fruits to turkeys. The turkeys crushed 7 of them. He planted the other 10 seeds, and 3 sprouted. Many people believed the story, and it went into books. But Temple had not planted any seeds that were not eaten, to compare. So nobody could tell whether the turkeys made any difference. Foresters in Mauritius pointed out that they had sprouted tambalacoque seeds before, with no bird at all, and that younger trees did exist. Later studies found the tree was dying out mainly because of pigs, monkeys and plants brought to the island by people.
how_we_found_out.who: Stanley Temple, an American scientist, and the foresters and botanists who questioned him, including those of Mauritius
how_we_found_out.when: 1977 (Temple's paper in the journal Science), questioned from 1979, and reviewed again in 1991 and 2004
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the tambalacoque tree's seeds could sprout only after passing through a dodo. Temple's test had no comparison group of uneaten seeds. Seeds were sprouted without any dodo, and young trees were found.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today, in a city flat, with the materials listed. The Juice Test needs only a ripe tomato, two tiffin or takeaway boxes, tissue and a tea strainer. Washed tomato seeds on wet tissue usually show roots in 3 to 6 days in a warm Indian home, so the test runs 8 days; the steps say what to do if the room is cold or the tomato was picked green. The juice for topping up is kept in the fridge, because juice left out ferments. Mould may grow in Box J: the safety note says not to sniff it and to bin it in a closed bag, and Waiting or Dead tells the parent to leave mouldy seeds out. Seeds don't need light to sprout, so the boxes stay closed on top of the fridge. Ripe or Green relies on fruit flies, which are common in Indian kitchens but not certain, so it is outside the spine and says to count ants or house flies instead. The rice-flour kolam needs real rice flour or rava, since chalk kolams feed nobody. Cup and Card practises on a paper beetle when no creature turns up, and a grown-up handles anything that might sting. The tomato project needs a balcony or window with at least 5 hours of sun; a shady window gives thin plants with few flowers. Timings were checked step by step. The spine (intro, the Fruit Bowl Question, the Juice Test set-up and daily checks, the explanation cards, Roots and the quiz) fits about 85 minutes over two sessions, plus 2 or 3 minutes a day of checking.
